sDescription: A court order was secured by Los Angeles law enforcement to prevent the medical examiner from making public records concerning the death of a 14-year-old female whose body was found inside the trunk of a Tesla belonging to singer D4vd in September. The victim, Celeste Rivas Hernandez, disappeared on Valentine's Day 2024, leading her family to submit a missing persons report the following day. On Sept. 8, investigators located the heavily decomposed body at a Hollywood tow facility. The vehicle had been removed from a Hollywood Hills roadway where it had been left abandoned for weeks.

American singer and actress Irene Cara passed away at age 63 due to hypertensive and arteriosclerotic heart disease. She gained widespread recognition playing Coco Hernandez in the 1980 musical film Fame and by performing its title track 'Fame', which secured the No. 1 position on charts across multiple nations. During 1983, Cara performed and co-authored 'Flashdance... What a Feeling' for the movie Flashdance, earning a shared Academy Award for Best Original Song alongside a Grammy Award for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance in 1984. Initially selected as a dancer for Fame, producers Alan Marshall and David Da Silva adjusted the part of Coco Hernandez specifically for her after discovering her vocal abilities.

Scottish singer-songwriter Iain Sutherland, co-writer of Sir Rod Stewart's 1975 hit 'Sailing', has passed away. Sutherland originally recorded the track with his brother Gavin in 1972 prior to its international success under Sir Rod. Initially performing together as the folk group Sutherland Brothers Band, the siblings subsequently merged with a local rock outfit named Quiver to form Sutherland Brothers & Quiver.

Massachusetts' highest court dismissed defamation lawsuits brought by Tom Scholz, founder of the rock group Boston, against the Boston Herald and the ex-wife of Brad Delp, the band's late lead singer. Scholz had initiated the legal action following the publication of articles by the Herald containing statements by Micki Delp that Scholz argued could be interpreted as holding him responsible for the 2007 suicide of Delp.

Don DeVito, a longtime Columbia Records executive who produced the key Bob Dylan albums Blood on the Tracks and Desire, passed away at the age of 72 following a 16-year fight against prostate cancer. Throughout his career, DeVito also collaborated with performers such as Bruce Springsteen, Billy Joel, and Aerosmith. His career began as a touring guitarist for Al Kooper, and he previously led his own group, The Sabres, which dissolved during a tour. Columbia stated that DeVito was left stranded in Fort Smith, Ark., when a chance meeting with Johnny Cash sparked a lifelong friendship, with Cash eventually introducing DeVito to Dylan.

An Antonio's restaurant was targeted by a prankster who ordered 178 pizzas under the pretense that they were intended for singer Bob Dylan and his entourage. The hoaxer, sporting a counterfeit pass for a Dylan concert, phoned the establishment to place the massive order valued at upwards of $3,900. The proprietor was informed that the pies were for Dylan and his crew following a concert appearance in Amherst, Massachusetts. Employees at Antonios labored until 5.30am preparing the order, only to be shocked when nobody showed up to pick it up.

At a ceremony in Feltham town centre, Brian May and Freddie Mercury's 87-year-old mother, Jer Bulsara, unveiled a plaque commemorating the late singer. More than 2,000 fans gathered at the Centre on Feltham High Street in England, with some traveling from as far as Australia and Japan. Inscribed as "Freddie Mercury - musician, singer and songwriter," the plaque also notes the dates he resided in Feltham from 1964 to 1968.

An amicable settlement concluded the legal battle regarding a music agreement involving Michael Jackson and an Arab sheik. Prior to an agreement in principle being established, Jackson was scheduled to travel to the United Kingdom to testify at the High Court. Sheikh Abdulla Bin Hamad Bin Isa Al-Khalifa, who is the son of the King of Bahrain, had initiated a lawsuit against Jackson seeking £4.7m and alleging that the artist failed to fulfill a music contract.

Kevin Dubrow, the frontman with metal band Quiet Riot, was found dead in his Las Vegas home at the age of 52. Their 1983 release Metal Health was the first metal album to top the US charts. The band's biggest hit was 'Cum on Feel the Noize', a cover of the Slade song which they are said to have grudgingly recorded in just one take.

Madonna earned her sixth No. 1 on the US album charts, marking her third consecutive chart-topping album in the US, with 'Confessions on a Dance Floor'. Setting a new record, the album reached No. 1 across 40 countries. This record was previously held by The Beatles, whose album 1 went to No. 1 in 36 countries in 2000 The Beatles.

Glen Campbell was taken into custody in Phoenix, Arizona, following a collision between his BMW and a Toyota Camry, registering a blood alcohol level of .20. The charges against him included 'extreme' drunk driving, hit and run, and assaulting an officer of the law. According to a police report, Campbell continuously hummed his successful track 'Rhinestone Cowboy' while he was being held.

After receiving a diagnosis for a condition resulting in an irregular heartbeat, Meat Loaf had heart surgery at a hospital in London. The collapse of the 52-year-old singer occurred on November 17th during a performance at Wembley Arena in London.

Michael Jackson launched a website to defend himself following allegations of sexual abuse of a 12-year old boy. The singer posted a message saying the charges were based on 'a big lie' and he wanted to end 'this horrible time' by proving they were false in court.

Robbie Williams began an eight-week tenure at No. 1 on the UK album chart with Swing When You're Winning. The release achieved a 7x Platinum certification, remained on the UK Albums Chart for 57 weeks, and secured the position of the 49th best-selling album in UK history.

A burglar entered the Paradise Valley residence of Alice Cooper and stole four of the star's gold discs, alongside more than $6000 in cameras, shoes, and clothing that belonged to the singer's daughter.

Sculptor Irena Sedlecka created a tribute monument to Freddie Mercury in Montreux, Switzerland. The nearly 10-foot (3-metre) tall structure faces Lake Geneva and was revealed by Montserrat Caballé alongside Freddie's father, with fellow band members Brian May and Roger Taylor present at the unveiling.
Whitney Houston achieved a US singles chart No. 1 with "Exhale (Shoop Shoop)". Composed by Babyface and featured in the movie "Waiting To Exhale", the track marked her 11th US No. 1.

Whitney Houston and Kevin Costner starred in the nationwide release of The Bodyguard. Lawrence Kasdan penned the movie in the 1970s as an intended starring project for Diana Ross and Steve McQueen, marking Houston's first film role. Globally, it ranked as the second-highest-grossing movie of 1992, and its accompanying soundtrack achieved the status of the top-selling soundtrack in history, with worldwide sales exceeding 42 million copies.

British pop stars assembled at S.A.R.M. Studios in London to record the historic single "Do They Know It's Christmas?". Midge Ure and Bob Geldof wrote the track, which included performances by Paul Young, Boy George, Bono, Sting, and George Michael. The release surpassed three million sales in the UK to become the bestselling record of all time, while generating more than £8 million ($13.6 million) globally.

The Band made their final performance; 'The Last Waltz' held on American Thanksgiving Day, at Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco. The show also featured Joni Mitchell, Dr John, Neil Young, Van Morrison, Neil Diamond, Eric Clapton and others. The event was filmed by director Martin Scorsese and made into a documentary of the same name, released in 1978.

UK singer and songwriter Nick Drake passed away in his sleep at the age of 26 following an overdose of the antidepressant tryptasol. Having signed with Island Records at the age of twenty, Drake recorded the 1972 album Pink Moon. Volkswagen used the title track from Pink Moon in a TV commercial in 2000, leading Drake to sell more records within a single month than he had over the preceding thirty years.

Chuck Berry topped the UK singles chart with 'My Ding a-Ling', which marked his sole No.1 single in the UK. Originally, Dave Bartholomew recorded the track in 1952. The recording of Berry's version took place during a concert on 3 February 1972 at the Locarno ballroom in Coventry, England. Jim Connors, a disc jockey for Boston radio station WMEX, received a gold record for finding the song and driving it to the top of the charts through radio airplay and his influence among American peers.
John Lennon sent his MBE back to The Queen, citing Britain's part in the Nigeria-Biafra conflict, American actions in Vietnam, and the downward chart movement of his newest single, 'Cold Turkey'.

The Jimi Hendrix Experience gave their first live performance in the UK at London's Bag O'Nails Club, utilizing the venue's DJ booth for their set. Regular visitors to the establishment included Eric Clapton, Pete Townshend, The Beatles, Mick Jagger, Brian Jones, Jeff Beck, Jimmy Page, The Hollies, and the Small Faces.

The Seekers achieved a No. 1 hit on the UK singles chart with 'The Carnival Is Over', which marked their second chart-topper. The track originated as an 1883 Russian folk song and features lyrics penned by Tom Springfield, the brother of Dusty Springfield. During its highest sales period, the single moved 93,000 copies daily and currently holds the No. 30 spot among the best-selling singles in United Kingdom history.
The The Beatles conducted their Christmas shopping privately after Harrods department store in London, England, closed its doors to the public.

Lord Rockinghams XI were at No.1 on the UK singles chart with 'Hoot's Mon', (based on the traditional Scottish folk song 'One Hundred Pipers'). Lord Rockingham's XI were the house band on the UK Jack Good TV show 'Oh Boy.'

British singer and songwriter of Nigerian descent Tunde Baiyewu, who with the Lighthouse Family, had the 1996 UK No.4 single 'Lifted' plus 9 other UK Top 40 singles. Their 1995 debut album Ocean Drive sold more than 1.8 million copies in the UK alone.

Rodney Sheppard is the guitarist for the American rock band Sugar Ray. In 1997, the group attained mainstream success with the pop-infused single 'Fly'. Their top-selling album, 14:59, came out in 1999.

American R&B singer Stacey Lattishaw, who had the 1980 US No.21 single 'Let Me Be Your Angel' and the 1980 UK No.3 single 'Jump to The Beat'. She signed with Motown in 1986. She scored her only No. 1 R&B hit with duet partner Johnny Gill, titled 'Where Do We Go from Here', in 1989.

Fernando and Nefty Sallaberry are singers and actors who belonged to the original lineup of the Puerto Rican boy band Menudo. Menudo has been ranked among the biggest boy bands of all time, with worldwide album sales estimated at 20 million.

American musician, songwriter, and record producer Tim Armstrong is recognized for his unique voice and serves as the singer and guitarist for the punk rock band Rancid alongside the hip-hop and punk rock supergroup Transplants. Beyond his primary bands, Armstrong writes songs for various other musicians. His professional collaborations include working with Joe Walsh and the Interrupters, and he earned a Grammy Award for his contributions to the work of Jimmy Cliff and Pink.

Mark Lanegan was an American alternative rock musician and singer-songwriter. He co-founded Screaming Trees and belonged to Queens of the Stone Age, appearing on five of their albums. Lanegan passed away on 22 February 2022 at the age of 57.

American singer-songwriter and musician Amy Grant achieved a 1991 US No.1 and UK No.2 single with 'Baby Baby'. By 2009, she had sold over 30 million albums globally and earned six Grammy Awards along with 22 Gospel Music Association Dove Awards. Additionally, Grant released the first Christian album to achieve platinum status.

Steve Rothery is the guitarist of the British rock band Marillion, known for the 1985 UK No.2 single 'Kayleigh'. Between 1983 and 1994, the group secured eight Top Ten UK albums, which included the 1985 No.1 album Misplaced Childhood.

Jocelyn Brown is an American R&B and dance singer. She landed a No.5 single in the UK in 1997 with 'Something Goin' On' and has collaborated with John Lennon, Bob Dylan, and Bruce Springsteen. Her vocals have featured on 23 hit singles on the UK singles chart, including eight entries that made the top 20.

English rock musician and Electric Light Orchestra drummer Bev Bevan previously played for The Move, scoring the 1969 UK No.1 single 'Blackberry Way'. Alongside his work with Electric Light Orchestra—which included the 1979 UK No.3 and US No.4 single 'Don't Bring Me Down' as well as 26 other Top 40 hits—Bevan also performed as the touring drummer for Black Sabbath during their 1983 Born Again Tour.

Bob Lind is an American playwright, novelist, and singer-songwriter who helped define the 1960s folk rock movement in the US and UK. His single 'Elusive Butterfly' became a No.5 hit in both the US and the UK in 1966.

Percy Sledge was an American R&B, soul and gospel singer. In 1966, he released the single 'When A Man Loves A Woman', which reached No. 1 in the US and No. 4 in the UK. His career experienced a renaissance during the 1980s when the track returned to the UK Singles Chart following its feature in a Levi's commercial, climbing to No. 2 behind a reissue of Ben E. King's classic 'Stand by Me'. Sledge was married twice and fathered twelve children. He passed away from liver cancer on April 14th 2015.
